standard.title: Abstract nouns and nominalisation for condensing
standard.description: understand how abstract nouns and nominalisation can be used to summarise ideas in text
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how complex and compound-complex sentences elaborate, extend and explain ideas (AC9E7LA05). They have encountered nominalisation as a cohesive device (AC9E9LA04). They have not yet focused specifically on how abstract nouns and nominalisation function to summarise and carry forward prior ideas within a text.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand how abstract nouns and nominalisation summarise ideas, structure arguments and allow texts to treat prior content as an established premise.

nodes.label: Abstract nouns as summary references
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify abstract nouns used to summarise prior text content and explain what they compress.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify two abstract nouns in an academic or informational text (e.g. 'the previous argument', 'the prologue') and explain what content each compresses from earlier in the text.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how abstract nouns in academic and technical texts function as backward-pointing summary references, distilling earlier explanations into a single noun phrase that can be treated as established.
wider: Compare how abstract nouns function differently in scientific texts versus literary criticism — and what this reveals about how different disciplines build knowledge
Examine how the absence of abstract summary nouns affects the coherence of student writing, using concrete examples

response_modes.reason: Abstract nouns used as summary references are common in academic and technical texts but uncommon in everyday writing. Students need exposure across disciplines to see this as a systematic knowledge-building device rather than incidental usage.

nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify abstract nouns as summary references cannot understand N2 — the argument-structuring function of nominalisation depends on first seeing that noun phrases carry condensed prior content. Without N1, the process→thing transformation at N2 has no conceptual anchor.
success_criteria: Student identifies an abstract noun used as a summary reference
Student explains what prior text content it compresses into the noun phrase

nodes.label: Nominalisation as argument structure
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how nominalisation structures an argument by transforming processes into things that can be positioned, qualified and built upon.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a nominalised form in an argument (e.g. 'the destruction of' instead of 'destroying') and explain how treating the process as a noun-thing advances the argument.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how nominalisations structure an argument in an academic or informational text, tracking how transformed processes become the objects of further reasoning.
wider: Compare two versions of the same paragraph — one with nominalisations, one with verb forms — and analyse the effect on argumentative density and register
Examine how nominalisation in political or bureaucratic texts can obscure who is doing what, and evaluate the effect on accountability

response_modes.reason: The grammatical transformation (process → thing) is abstract. Students need the reasoning scaffold: verb form → nominalised form → what this allows the sentence to do next. Without this chain, students see nominalisations as vocabulary choices rather than structural ones.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The connection between nominalisation and accountability/ideology — who disappears from the text when processes become things — is genuinely enriching for Year 9 critical literacy. This is conceptually rich width that connects language and power without being senior-level content.
success_criteria: Student identifies a nominalised form and states the process verb it derives from
Student explains what grammatical advantage the nominalised form gives the writer (e.g. positioning as subject, adding qualifier, advancing the argument)
